learning: If this race again matches iterations 0 to 2 to four decimals, treat the race pipeline as repeating data and stop changing geometry or gains until it is checked. If the metrics differ, the change is from wheel_track: check max_error against 0.06 m, line_loss_events, and steering_oscillation, which should rise if yaw response is now too strong.
notes: Iteration 3 package: the Builder's wheel_track 0.10 m test, with the controller held at the iteration-2 gains so the track is the only change. The controller is unchanged because iterations 0 to 2 gave identical metrics and no new gain evidence exists.
rationale: The Builder's iteration-3 geometry changes only wheel_track, from 0.12 m to 0.10 m, and keeps the 16 mm footprint and the 0.03 m spread from iteration 2. Iterations 0, 1 and 2 gave identical race metrics to four decimals on all three tracks (score 26.0449, max_error about 0.061 m, one line-loss event per trial, 0% finish). Three different geometry changes (spread 0.02 to 0.03 m, footprint 12 to 16 mm, and sensor weights rescaled) produced no change, so the race pipeline may be repeating data. Until a new result differs from those rows, I cannot attribute any effect to geometry or controller. The controller therefore stays identical to iteration 2 (kp 2.0, ki 0, kd 0.05, base_speed 1.6, weights x/0.02, last_direction), so that any change in the next race comes from the wheel_track alone. Narrowing the track from 0.12 m to 0.10 m raises yaw per unit of PWM difference by about 20 percent (turn rate = wheel speed difference / wheel_track), so the robot should turn harder at the same turn command. The risk is more steering_oscillation, which the observation request will show. Sensor geometry, body, wheel radius and mass are unchanged from the Builder's proposal. The observation request keeps the full measurement set, which lets the Builder see line losses, max_error and oscillation together.
